After spending the day doing some more research, I think protective coatings could become HydroGraph’s most profitable application.

The attraction is the combination of customer savings, meaningful graphene volumes and potential recurring demand.

For the owner of a ship, industrial plant or offshore structure, corrosion means repairs, surface preparation, labour and downtime. A coating that reduces maintenance could create savings well beyond its purchase price. That gives an effective additive a strong economic argument.

HydroGraph already has encouraging evidence. Initial Sparc laboratory tests incorporating its FGA-1 into commercial water-based coatings showed 39–60% less corrosion creep during testing lasting up to 1,680 hours. The collaboration covers further testing and potential commercial supply.

Then consider the quantities.

HydroGraph’s white paper describes 0.5% graphene in one polyurethane coating formulation, compared with 0.0015% in PET bottle testing.

For an illustrative 10,000 tonnes of finished product, those concentrations represent:

• Coating formulation: 50 tonnes of graphene
• PET formulation: 150 kg of graphene

That is approximately 333 times more graphene per tonne of finished product in the coating example.
These are separate test formulations; commercial doses and prices will vary. Still, they show why a coating application could generate substantial material demand without requiring adoption across an entire global industry.

HydroGraph’s aqueous paste also offers manufacturers a practical route into water-based formulations using standard mixing equipment.

Protective coatings could combine meaningful graphene volumes with customers willing to pay for lower maintenance costs and longer asset life. Successful formulations adopted by established manufacturers could generate repeat orders across years of production. That is why I believe a handful of commercial wins could make coatings HydroGraph’s most profitable application and a major driver of shareholder value.

HydroGraph’s share price has fallen sharply. My view of the fundamentals remains unchanged: I haven’t seen a disclosed setback that breaks the investment thesis.

The GEIC customer pipeline, qualified compounding partners and funded US expansion remain the foundations of that case.

And management’s commercial target deserves attention.

The August MD&A explicitly anticipated BOTH larger purchase orders and a long-term supply agreement within calendar 2026, arising from customer development through the GEIC. The CEO subsequently reiterated expectations for first commercial contracts this year, with the biggest ramp-up in 2027.

Unless HydroGraph revises that outlook, I still expect those milestones before year-end, roughly eleven weeks away. They remain expectations, with execution still to be demonstrated.

The GEIC connection matters. These potential orders would emerge from existing customer projects, where years of formulation, testing and industrial trials could finally translate into commercial purchasing.

My first guess is plastics or packaging, potentially through a qualified compounder such as Broadway or Hubron.

I’m particularly watching the Duo/QVC supply chain. Duo’s GEIC-developed 2DPE graphene packaging is already being used commercially for QVC. That makes it an intriguing candidate, but HydroGraph’s involvement has not been confirmed, so this is explicitly my speculation.

Larger orders would demonstrate growing demand. A meaningful long-term agreement could add visibility into repeat business.

𝗡𝗕𝗔 𝗦𝗰𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴

Less than a year ago, I warned about nine of the most hyped growth stocks on X:

$IONQ, $RGTI, $QBTS, $IREN, $QUBT, $OSCR, $HIMS, $ACHR, $OKLO.

Eight of them have since fallen an average of 45%. One is up 130%.

The entire equal-weighted basket is down 26%, while $QQQ is up 17% over the same period. That’s 43 percentage points of underperformance.

People think successful investing requires a lot of work. I think it requires something more important: 𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰.

Let me explain how growth investing works through NBA scouting.

Imagine you’re an NBA scout, looking for future basketball stars.

𝗞𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗻: You find ten kids who are absolutely destroying everyone around them. They’re faster, stronger, and more talented. They look like future NBA superstars.

You get excited. You invest in them. The charts go up.

𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝘀𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗹: Most of your ten kids are still excellent players. They’re outperforming almost everyone around them. Their reputations grow, and so do their valuations. The charts still look amazing.

𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗲: Now the competition becomes much tougher. A few of your stars are no longer that special. Others are still doing very well. Most have been winners for so long that everyone assumes they will continue winning.

The charts look great. Expectations are enormous.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝗕𝗔: Reality finally arrives.

Out of the ten kids you identified in kindergarten, maybe one becomes an NBA superstar. A couple might have decent professional careers. The rest never make it. They go on to live perfectly normal lives, working regular jobs. Nobody remembers how incredible they looked in kindergarten.

And that’s exactly how growth investing works.

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.

You’re not an NBA scout.

You’re not a professional who has spent his entire career identifying promising talent before everyone else, just like a hedge fund manager who spends his life looking for the next great company.

You don’t discover these kids in kindergarten.

If you’re lucky, you discover them in high school. But most retail investors discover them in college.

By then, they’re already famous. Everyone is talking about them. Their charts look incredible. Their valuations already reflect years of expected future success.

You buy them because they’ve been winning for years. Their stories sound amazing. Everyone agrees they’re going to be superstars.

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂’𝗿𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗲 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿 𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝗡𝗕𝗔 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

And then comes the NBA.

Suddenly, most of your superstars turn out to be average players. Some don’t even make the league.

The problem isn’t necessarily that these companies are bad businesses. Some might become very successful companies.

The problem is that you paid for greatness before greatness was proven.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗸 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗰�� 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆. 𝗜𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄.

And when you pay NBA superstar prices for a talented college player, even a very good career can become a terrible investment.

How do you value a blockchain?

Most people try to run a discounted cash flow model on it, like its a company. Ive had that argument plenty of times over the years and its nonsense.

Invert it instead.

Imagine you switch Ethereum off tomorrow. Every stablecoin on it, all of DeFi, every layer 2, every NFT... all of it goes to zero in an instant. Everything that would disappear is what Ethereum is actually worth.

The reason these networks attract so much capital is that they are dense with intelligence. Ethereum has the most developers, its programmable, it has the deepest markets and the whole ecosystem built on top of it. Solana and Sui are faster, cheaper, more efficient, with different feature sets...

Turn it off and see what breaks. Thats the valuation.

More agentic activity onchain makes the whole thing go exponential
